title: Dawn Practice: Girls' Cricket in Mumbai
focus: Past simple, present perfect and contrast
paragraphs: At six in the morning, while most of Mumbai is still asleep, forty girls are already running laps around a dusty ground between two apartment blocks. Some wear school shoes; one wears flip-flops. The coach, a former bank clerk named Sunil Patil, blows a whistle and shouts, 'Again!' Nobody complains.

The girls' team started three years ago, when Sunil noticed that his daughter, Shreya, was always sent to fetch the ball but never allowed to bat. 'The boys said cricket was not for girls,' he recalls. 'I asked myself who made that rule.' He put up a handwritten notice at the local market, inviting any girl aged ten to sixteen to come on Sunday morning. Four arrived.

Today there are forty, and the club has two teams. The equipment is mostly donated or second-hand: bats repaired with tape, pads that once belonged to a boys' school, and a single helmet that is passed around between batters. Families pay a monthly contribution of one hundred rupees, but those who cannot afford it are not asked to pay.

Not everyone has been supportive. Meena Shaikh, fifteen, remembers that her uncle told her father to keep her at home and 'concentrate on her exams'. 'My father listened to him for a month,' she says. 'Then he came to watch one match, and he never missed another.'

The results on the field have been modest: the team has won seven matches and lost eleven. Yet Sunil is not concerned about the scoreboard. He points out that attendance at school among the players has been consistently high, and that several of the older girls now help to coach the younger ones. 'A team teaches you to lose without disappearing,' he says. 'That's more useful than any trophy.'

The club's dream is to find a permanent ground, since residents of the apartment blocks sometimes complain about broken windows. Last month, a local councillor promised to discuss the problem. Meanwhile, the girls continue to run their laps, keeping one eye on the windows. 'We aim carefully,' Meena says with a grin. 'Mostly.'

title: Review: Small Hours
paragraphs: Most podcasts want to be heard on the way to work. Small Hours, a new series from independent producer Noor Hassan, wants to be heard at three in the morning, when you cannot sleep and the house is quiet. Its premise is simple: each episode, Noor talks with someone who works at night.

The guests are ordinary and extraordinary at once: a baker in Cairo who begins to knead dough at midnight, a night nurse in Manila, a lorry driver crossing the Chilean desert, a security guard who writes poetry between his rounds. Noor asks few questions and leaves long pauses, so that the guests, who might never be interviewed otherwise, fill the silence with remarkably honest thoughts.

The strongest episode, in my opinion, is the one with Ana, a radio presenter in Buenos Aires who answers calls from lonely listeners until dawn. She describes a regular caller, an elderly man who phones every night only to say good evening and hang up. 'I used to think he was wasting my time,' she says. 'Now I know that I was the only person he spoke to that day.' I had to stop the episode and take a deep breath.

The production deserves praise. There is no music, only the natural sounds of each place: the oven doors of the bakery, the beeping of hospital machines, the wind on the desert road. At first this seems austere, but it creates an intimacy that no soundtrack could imitate. Headphones are strongly recommended.

However, the series is not perfect. A few episodes feel too long, and one interview, with a night-club doorman, is so full of stories about celebrities that it loses the human warmth of the others. Noor also tends to agree with her guests too quickly; a more challenging question here and there would have given the episodes more depth.

Still, these are small faults in a series with a distinctive voice. Each episode lasts about thirty minutes, which makes it ideal for a bus ride or for the hour before bed. Do not expect to be entertained in the usual way. Expect, instead, to be reminded that the world is kept running by people we rarely see. Highly recommended.

title: Calm Voices on the Mountain: A Rescue Volunteer Speaks
focus: Reported speech and modals of advice
paragraphs: Roxana Huamán is twenty-eight, works as a physiotherapist in Huaraz, in the Peruvian Andes, and, in her free time, volunteers for a mountain rescue team. We met her after a long weekend spent searching for two lost hikers.
Q: How did you join the team?

A: Through an accident, actually. Six years ago, I broke my ankle on a trek, and the rescuers carried me down for five hours. I couldn't stop thinking about how calm they were. When I recovered, I asked how to join, and they said, 'First, learn to walk properly.' We all laughed, but they were serious.
Q: What does the training involve?

A: Mainly first aid, rope work and navigation. We also practise something less obvious: talking to frightened people. If a hiker is panicking, the best medicine is a steady voice. We have a rule: never say 'don't worry'. It never works. Instead, say what you are going to do, step by step.
Q: What is the most common cause of rescues?

A: Honestly, bad planning. People start walking late in the afternoon, wear cotton clothes, or carry too little water. The weather changes quickly here, and a sunny morning can become a snowstorm by lunch. Most accidents could be prevented if hikers checked the forecast and told someone where they were going.
Q: Is it ever frustrating?

A: Sometimes. Last year we spent a whole night looking for a group who had simply decided to camp somewhere else and forgotten to tell anyone. When we found them, they were cooking soup and asked if we wanted some. I wanted to be angry, but I was too tired, and, to be fair, the soup was good.
Q: Do you get paid?
A: No, we are all volunteers, and we buy much of our own equipment. A good pair of boots costs a lot, but nobody has ever left because of money.
Q: What would you like people to know?

A: That asking for help is not a weakness. The tragedies I've seen usually began with someone who was too proud to turn back. A summit will be there next year. You might not be. Come home, and try again.

title: Fewer Places, Deeper Journeys
paragraphs: A friend of mine once visited seven countries in ten days. She has the photographs to prove it: a tower here, a bridge there, and in each picture, the same slightly tired smile. When I asked what she remembered best, she thought for a long time and answered, 'The airport in Frankfurt.'

It would be easy to laugh at her, but most of us have done something similar. Cheap flights, tight schedules and the fear of 'missing' something encourage us to treat travel as a list to be completed. The result is often a collection of places we have seen but never really visited.

Slow travel offers a different philosophy. The idea is simple: go to fewer places, stay longer and move by the most direct and humane means available, often by train, bus or even on foot. Rather than hurry from monument to monument, you try to live in a place for a few days, shopping at the same market, greeting the same neighbour and, if you are lucky, getting a little lost.

The benefits are surprising. First, it is usually cheaper, since you spend less on transport and more time in modest guesthouses and local cafés. Second, it is kinder to the environment, as trains and buses produce fewer emissions than planes on most short routes. Third, and most importantly, it changes the quality of your memories. A conversation with a baker on your fourth morning will stay with you longer than a monument seen for twenty minutes.

Naturally, slow travel is not always possible. People with only one week's holiday cannot spend three days crossing a country by bus, and some regions have poor public transport. It would also be unfair to claim that fast travel is always shallow; a short weekend can be wonderful if it is well chosen. The point is not to follow a rule but to ask a question: what do I want from this journey?

If the answer is 'photographs', fine. But if it is 'to understand something', then perhaps the best plan is to book fewer tickets, pack a lighter bag and allow time for the unexpected. After all, the most interesting part of a trip is often the part that was not planned.

title: The Piano on Platform Four
paragraphs: The piano had been standing on Platform Four of the station for two weeks, and nobody knew who had put it there. A small sign taped to its lid read, 'Play me. I'm free.' Every commuter hurried past it with their eyes on their phone. Kofi Mensah, a night-shift cleaner who finished work at seven, was the first person to lift the lid.

Kofi had not touched a piano in thirty years. As a boy in Accra, he had taken lessons from a strict neighbour, and he had hated every minute, especially the scales. But that morning, tired and alone on the platform, he pressed a single key. The note rang out under the iron roof, clear and unexpectedly beautiful.

He played a clumsy version of a hymn his mother used to sing. A schoolgirl stopped to listen, then a man in a suit, then two builders carrying coffee. By the time Kofi finished, there were a dozen people standing around him, and none of them was looking at a phone. He felt the heat rise to his face. 'Sorry,' he muttered, 'I'm out of practice.' The schoolgirl smiled. 'Do another one,' she said.

After that, he came every morning. He bought a songbook for four pounds from a charity shop and practised a new tune each week on the platform for twenty minutes before going home. Little by little, other people began to leave small things on the piano: a flower, a handwritten note saying 'thank you', a bar of chocolate. A woman who sold sandwiches from a cart brought him a free coffee each Friday.

One Monday, the piano was gone. The station manager explained that it had been moved to a warehouse because of safety rules. Kofi felt the loss more than he expected. For the first time in weeks, he walked straight past the empty space, and the platform seemed louder and colder than before.

Three days later, a new notice appeared where the piano had stood. It said that the instrument would return the following month, with a proper cover and a small plaque. At the bottom, in pencil, somebody had added: 'Kofi, we saved you a seat.' He read it twice. Then he laughed, folded his songbook under his arm, and, for the first time in thirty years, looked forward to a Monday.

title: Community Garden Pilot: Evaluation Report
paragraphs: ## Background

This report evaluates a three-month pilot project in which students at Instituto Nuevo Horizonte in Panama City created a community garden in a disused corner of the school grounds. The project was proposed by the Year 10 science class, and it was supervised by a biology teacher.
## Activities

The garden measures roughly forty square metres and contains twelve raised beds. Each class was responsible for one raised bed. Students planted tomatoes, peppers, basil and beans, and they built a compost bin using food waste from the cafeteria. A rota ensured that the plants were watered every day, including weekends, when volunteers took turns.
## Results

After three months, the garden produced about 35 kilograms of vegetables, most of which were donated to a nearby community kitchen. Beans were the most successful crop, while tomatoes suffered from insects and produced less than expected. A survey of the 60 participating students found that 48 of them (80 per cent) felt more interested in science lessons, and 51 (85 per cent) said they would recommend the project to other schools. The total cost was 410 dollars, of which 300 were covered by a donation from a local hardware shop. The remaining 110 dollars came from the school's budget.
## Problems

Two main difficulties were identified. First, watering during the dry season depended entirely on volunteers, and several beds were neglected during the holidays. Second, some students lost motivation after the first month, once the novelty had disappeared.
## Conclusion and recommendations

The pilot can be considered a success, although its benefits were more educational than financial. It is worth noting, however, that the sample consists only of students who took part, so their opinions may be more positive than those of the school as a whole. We recommend extending the project for a full school year, installing a simple irrigation system, and involving parents in holiday maintenance. A rainwater tank would also reduce water costs, which, although low, are not zero.

title: A Letter to the Editor About Scooters
paragraphs: Dear Editor,

I am writing in response to your article 'Scooters: Freedom or Menace?', published last week. As a nineteen-year-old who uses an electric scooter every day to travel between my home in Carabanchel and my university in the centre of Madrid, I felt that the article presented a rather one-sided picture.

It is true that some riders behave irresponsibly. I have seen scooters on the pavement, ridden by people with headphones in both ears, and I understand why pedestrians feel threatened. Last month, I almost hit a toddler who ran out of a shop; I managed to brake in time, but my heart was racing for an hour. That experience convinced me that rules are necessary. However, to blame the scooters themselves is like blaming cars for dangerous drivers. The problem lies in the lack of clear rules and in the absence of enforcement.

For me, the scooter is not a toy. I paid 300 euros for it, an amount I will have recovered in fifteen months, because I save roughly twenty euros a month compared with taking the bus. I also arrive ten minutes earlier. For students on a small budget, that difference matters.

I would therefore propose three measures. First, riders should be required to wear helmets, as cyclists often are on busy roads. Second, the city should create a protected lane on every main road, so that scooters and pedestrians do not have to share narrow pavements. Third, there should be a registration system, with a small fine for those who park in doorways or ride where they should not.

Your article quoted several residents who dislike scooters, but did not interview a single user. I suspect that a conversation between the two groups would reveal that they want much the same thing: safe, calm streets. I would be happy to take part in such a discussion, should you decide to organise one.
Thank you for considering my letter.
Yours faithfully,
Álvaro Benítez

title: Why I Prefer Subtitles to Dubbing
paragraphs: Last Friday, I watched a Korean thriller in a cinema in Santiago with Spanish subtitles. The film was excellent, by the way. The girl next to me asked her friend, in a loud whisper, why the actors 'sounded so strange'. Her friend explained that the film was in its original language. I was tempted to join their conversation, because I have strong views on this topic: films should be watched with subtitles, not dubbed.

The first reason is authenticity. An actor's voice is not decoration; it is part of the performance. A trembling whisper, an angry silence, a laugh that breaks halfway: these are choices. When another person's voice replaces them, even the best dubbing actors can only imitate what was intended.

The second reason is language learning. Listening to English, Korean or Portuguese while reading a translation helps the ear to recognise rhythm, intonation and common phrases. I am not suggesting that you will become fluent by watching films, but it is surprising how much vocabulary one absorbs without noticing. In my own case, most of my first English phrases came from series.

Opponents raise legitimate objections. Reading subtitles can distract from the image, particularly in a fast action scene, and children who cannot yet read quickly would be excluded entirely. Moreover, good dubbing is a real craft, and many people have grown up with dubbed voices that they love as much as the originals. I have no wish to insult those who work in that profession.

Nevertheless, I believe the distraction argument is exaggerated. After the first ten minutes, the eyes learn to move automatically between the text and the picture, and most viewers stop noticing the subtitles at all. For children, the solution is simple: dubbed versions for young ages, subtitles from adolescence onward.

In a world where stories travel across borders in seconds, hearing the original voices is a small way of showing respect for their creators. It also reminds us that people elsewhere speak differently, laugh differently, and still tell stories that make us cry at exactly the same moments. That, for me, is worth reading a few lines.

title: The Bookshop on the Canal
paragraphs: In a quiet canal in the north of Amsterdam, between a rusty houseboat and a line of bicycles chained to a bridge, a green barge is moored with a blackboard on its deck. The board reads: 'Books. Tea. Cats.' Below, in smaller letters, someone has added: 'Please mind the water.'

The bookshop, called The Floating Page, belongs to Anneke Jansen, who is Dutch, and her partner Dayo Adeyemi, who moved from Lagos eight years ago. They bought the barge, which was once used to carry coal, for a price they prefer to keep secret, and spent two years converting it. Today, nearly four thousand second-hand books, in six languages, line the walls of its hold.

Customers step down a short wooden staircase and duck beneath a low beam, which has been painted yellow after too many bumped heads. Inside, there is a stove for winter, two armchairs and a sleepy cat named Comma, who is the only member of staff who never sells anything.

Why would anyone open a bookshop on the water? 'Because the rent in the city centre was impossible,' Anneke admits. 'A barge costs less to run, and the mooring fee is a fraction of a shop's rent.' She then adds more seriously, 'But also because people behave differently here. They speak quietly. They stay longer. A bookshop should feel like a place you can get lost in.'

The business is not without problems. In winter, the boat is cold and damp, and the books must be checked regularly for mould. Every spring, the barge needs to be lifted out of the water for repairs, which costs several thousand euros. Last year, the couple organised a crowdfunding campaign, and more than three hundred readers sent small donations.

In return, the shop offers its supporters a 'lifetime cup of tea', which, Dayo jokes, has so far cost them far more than expected. On Saturdays, they hold readings on the deck, with the audience sitting on cushions and, occasionally, on the neighbours' boats. 'We never planned a community,' says Anneke. 'We just left the door open. The rest happened by itself.'

options: It is formal and silent
It is noisy and busy
It is calm and welcoming
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: hay sillones, estufa, un gato, la gente 'speak quietly' y 'stay longer'; el ambiente es tranquilo y acogedor.

questions.q: Why does the author call Comma 'the only member of staff who never sells anything'?
options: To add humour to the description
To criticise the staff
To explain how the shop earns money
questions.explain_es: Propósito: es una broma ligera dentro de la descripción del local; no pretende criticar ni explicar el negocio.

questions.q: In 'a green barge is moored', 'moored' means…
options: painted a bright colour
lifted out of the water
tied up in one place
questions.explain_es: La barcaza está en un canal tranquilo y funciona como librería; 'moored' significa amarrada en un sitio.
